units.title: 四级匹配：社区钟表工坊的维修记录
units.instruction: Read the complete article. Match each statement to paragraph A–K. A paragraph may be used more than once or not at all.

materials.title: When a Clock Comes to the Workshop
materials.text:
This is an original fictional case for reading practice.

A

The first clock brought to the new Ash Lane workshop arrived in a shopping bag. Its owner wanted to hear the sound she remembered from childhood. The volunteers had expected simple requests to make clocks tell the right time, but their conversations soon covered family memories, appearance and the wish to keep an object in use. They decided that accepting a clock should begin with a question about what the owner hoped to achieve, rather than an immediate promise that every mechanism could be made to run again.

B

At the receiving desk, volunteers photographed existing cracks and loose pieces before any work began. These pictures helped distinguish earlier damage from a change noticed later. Every clock received an intake number, but the number meant only that the workshop had recorded it. It did not prove that the person who brought it was its legal owner. When there was a dispute about ownership, volunteers paused the work and asked the people concerned to resolve it outside the repair process. A repair record was not an ownership certificate.

C

The workshop’s public display included one clock with its hands permanently still. Visitors sometimes offered to wind it, thinking the volunteers had forgotten. A label explained that the case was original but the movement was too fragile for repeated demonstration. A modern teaching mechanism beside it showed how the hands moved. Keeping the historic clock stopped was therefore a deliberate choice. The volunteers could explain its operation without repeatedly stressing the material they were trying to preserve. The working model and the old object served different purposes.

D

Beginners could attend evening sessions, but attending did not authorise them to take apart any clock on the shelves. A trained volunteer first discussed the particular mechanism and decided which tasks were suitable. Some stored parts could move unexpectedly when released. The class therefore used selected teaching materials for early practice, while owners’ clocks remained under the responsibility of assigned repairers. The workshop did not treat enthusiasm as a substitute for preparation. A learner who had practised cleaning a case still needed separate guidance before attempting unfamiliar internal work.

E

One visitor described a brass clock as a wedding gift from an aunt. There was no dated letter or receipt to confirm that story. The workshop recorded the account in the owner’s words and identified it as a family recollection. Volunteers did not erase it because it lacked paperwork, but they did not turn it into a verified manufacturing date either. The note could preserve the object’s personal meaning while leaving a future reader free to distinguish an attributed memory from a fact supported by a document.

F

A tall fixed bench had made close work difficult for several participants, including a wheelchair user. The workshop bought a table whose height could be changed and moved some shared tools within easier reach. It then asked people to try actual tasks at the table. Merely measuring the available doorway would not have shown whether someone could comfortably examine a small part or use a lamp. The new arrangement was kept adjustable because a comfortable height for one participant was not necessarily the right height for another.

G

Finding a replacement part involved more than matching its general appearance. Two wheels could have the same outer diameter but different teeth. A volunteer measured the relevant dimensions and checked how a proposed part would interact with the mechanism. Removed originals were placed in a labelled bag linked to the intake number. They were not silently thrown into a mixed box of useful scraps. Keeping them allowed another repairer to see what had been changed and gave the owner a record of material removed from the clock.

H

Estimates separated work needed for reliable movement from optional changes to appearance. One owner wanted a scratched case polished until it shone; another preferred the marks left by years of use. Neither preference could be inferred from a request to repair the clock. The volunteer explained the choices and their costs before proceeding. A low initial price that quietly excluded requested work could be as misleading as a high total that included decorative treatment no one had asked for. Approval concerned a described set of tasks, not a vague promise of improvement.

I

Apprentices kept a shared notebook of adjustments and results. When a suggested change made a clock less accurate, the entry stayed in place with a later correction beside it. The notebook was intended to show what had actually been tried, not to create an uninterrupted story of success. A new apprentice could then avoid repeating an unsuccessful adjustment under the same conditions. Volunteers warned, however, that one mechanism’s response did not establish a rule for every clock of a similar appearance. The notes helped questions travel, as well as answers.

J

Occasionally a repaired clock was lent to the community hall for an exhibition. The loan agreement specified its position away from a frequently opened exterior door and named the person responsible for winding it. Hall staff could not assume that permission to display it included permission to move it to another wall. If the agreed place became unavailable, they contacted the workshop before changing the arrangement. The aim was not to forbid every practical adjustment, but to ensure that a change in conditions was noticed by someone familiar with the object.

K

At the end of the season, the workshop counted completed jobs but also reviewed requests it had declined or left unfinished. A clock kept safely stopped might represent a better result than one made to run briefly at the cost of further damage. The volunteers therefore resisted ranking their work by the number of ticking clocks alone. Their report described different outcomes and the reasons behind them. This gave supporters a less dramatic total, but a clearer view of what care for an object had meant in particular cases.

questions.prompt: Removed components were kept in a way that linked them to the object they came from.
questions.explanation: G明说原部件装入带接收号的袋，供后人核改动。B接收照记录先前损伤，不涉及拆下零件保管；其他段无该追溯袋。

questions.prompt: A separate working model allowed an old object to remain out of operation.
questions.explanation: C旧钟停走、现代教学机芯演示，两者功能分开。D是初学者材料权限，不是以工作模型替代古钟反复演示；其他段不含此安排。

questions.prompt: An unsuccessful adjustment remained visible together with its later correction.
questions.explanation: I共享笔记保留失准调整并旁注修正。G保管实物部件而非笔记错误；其他段未记录失败调整。

questions.prompt: Pictures were taken before work to document damage already present.
questions.explanation: B接收时先拍裂痕松件以区分前后损伤。G测量替换件无拍照步骤；其他段不含维修前损伤图像。

questions.prompt: Repair estimates distinguished functional work from optional changes to appearance.
questions.explanation: H明确区分走时工作与外观选项、先说成本。A先问目标但无分项估价；其他段未作费用划分。

questions.prompt: Participation in a class did not automatically permit work on every stored object.
questions.explanation: D上晚课不等于可拆所有架上钟，须具体指导和分配。F改善操作空间不授维修权限；其他段无此授权边界。

questions.prompt: A change to the work surface was assessed through actual tasks rather than doorway measurements alone.
questions.explanation: F可调桌高、实作试用，与仅量门口对照。J规定展墙环境而非工作桌可达性；其他段无桌面调整。

questions.prompt: An intake identifier was explicitly distinguished from evidence of legal ownership.
questions.explanation: B接收号只证明记录过，非物权证书；有争议暂停。E家族记忆真实性不讨论合法所有权；其他段无编号与产权区分。

questions.prompt: Permission to exhibit an object did not include unrestricted freedom to change its location.
questions.explanation: J展借约定位置，另移墙须先联系工坊。C静态展示关乎脆弱机芯，不是借出位置许可；其他段无搬位条件。

questions.prompt: An undocumented personal account was kept while being labelled as a recollection.
questions.explanation: E保留婚礼礼物口述并注明家族回忆，不等同核证日期。I是维修实验笔记，B是损伤照片，其他段不含此口述归属。

units.title: 四级匹配：渡船失物室的领取流程
units.instruction: Read the complete article. Match each statement to paragraph A–K. A paragraph may be used more than once or not at all.

materials.title: The Room Behind the Ticket Desk
materials.text:
This is an original fictional case for reading practice.

A

The small ferry terminal at Mill Reach once kept found property in a drawer beside the ticket machine. As passenger numbers rose, the drawer filled with bottles, coats and electronic devices. Staff moved the collection to a room behind the desk and wrote a procedure for recording and returning it. The change was less about buying larger shelves than about answering a difficult question: how could staff help the right person recover an object without giving it to someone who merely recognised a public description?

B

Each record named the boat or waiting area where an item had been found, along with the reported finding time. Staff distinguished this from the time it reached the office. A coat might be discovered during the morning crossing but delivered by a crew member only at the end of a shift. The record did not describe the place as the location of a theft, because staff usually did not know why the item had been left behind. Recording a fact did not justify inventing an explanation for it.

C

A ferry ticket could show that a claimant had travelled, but it did not establish ownership of a particular suitcase. Staff asked for details that had not been advertised publicly, such as an object packed inside or an unusual mark. They compared the account with the item in private. The procedure did not require every traveller to remember an exact brand name, since a detailed description of contents might be more helpful. Staff considered the combined evidence instead of treating possession of one ticket as a universal proof.

D

Food required a different response from a durable object. Staff would not keep a leaking lunch container on a shelf beside phones and clothing for the full ordinary storage period. They documented its disposal and the reason, while preserving enough of the record to answer a later enquiry. Valuable small objects were secured in a separate cabinet. These arrangements addressed different risks: contamination in one case, loss or unauthorised access in another. They were not a ranking of how much the missing owner cared about the item.

E

Passengers could enquire at the counter, by telephone or through an online form. A person who had difficulty using the form could describe the loss to a staff member, who entered it into the same system. This made the reporting route more accessible. It did not weaken the later ownership check: a clear phone conversation was not automatically stronger evidence than a typed message, and the choice of channel was not treated as a measure of honesty. Contact information was used to continue the enquiry, not to judge the claimant’s character.

F

The public noticeboard listed general categories, such as a dark backpack, rather than every distinctive detail. Some features had to remain unknown to the public so they could be used during verification. Photographs showing addresses, bank cards or identifying papers were not displayed. Staff could describe an item sufficiently to prompt an enquiry without publishing the private contents of someone’s bag. In particular, a scratch mentioned in a claimant’s account could help only if the noticeboard had not already told every passer-by exactly where to look.

G

A ring of keys presented a special difficulty because its owner might recognise a key without knowing its make. Where appropriate, staff arranged a supervised check with another identifying detail rather than simply handing over the entire collection for a passenger to try elsewhere. The aim was to add relevant evidence while keeping the item controlled until the claim was resolved. This procedure also avoided treating every key that looked similar as belonging to the same person. Appearance could begin an enquiry without completing it.

H

The terminal’s local policy allowed certain unclaimed textiles to be donated after a stated holding period. Staff recorded the date on which each eligible item was received and the date it left the store. They did not move everything out on one convenient afternoon without checking how long it had been held. Electronics and documents were handled through separate procedures. The notice explained this local arrangement to passengers; it did not pretend that the same rules necessarily applied at every ferry port or railway station.

I

Some enquiries concerned items lost on a connecting bus rather than the boat. Staff kept a current contact list for the bus operator and explained that the two services maintained separate records. Forwarding the enquiry could help a passenger reach the right office, but it did not mean the ferry team had searched the bus company’s store. The reply therefore named which records had actually been checked. This avoided an apparently reassuring statement that an item had been checked everywhere when only one operator’s list had been examined.

J

Shift changes created the risk that two staff members would separately promise the same object to different callers. The handover list therefore included unresolved claims and the evidence still needed. An item marked as under review remained in the room until the designated person had made a decision. A new shift did not begin the ownership check from nothing, nor assume that a friendly conversation recorded by the previous team meant release had already been authorised. The list carried the state of the enquiry, not just the physical item’s shelf position.

K

The first monthly report divided returns by the period in which items had arrived. An object found on the last afternoon of the month had had much less time to be claimed than one found four weeks earlier. Simply dividing all returns by all arrivals could obscure that difference. The terminal also distinguished enquiries closed after a return from enquiries still being investigated. An unresolved claim was not necessarily a failed return. These details made the report longer, but prevented a tidy percentage from suggesting that every case had reached a final outcome.

questions.prompt: Private information visible in an object was withheld from the public display.
questions.explanation: F明确不展示地址、银行卡或身份证明的照片。E收集联系方式供联系但不谈公开物件图像；其他段无公开图像隐私规则。

questions.prompt: An unresolved claim’s progress was passed between staff rather than lost at a shift change.
questions.explanation: J交接清单保留待决领取及还需证据，非只列架位。B是物品发现记录不涉及班次交接；其他段无此状态转交。

questions.prompt: Proof of a journey was not accepted as sufficient proof of ownership of an item.
questions.explanation: C船票能证坐船，不能独证箱子归属。G试钥匙为具体核验方式，不涉及船票证据；其他段无旅程证明区别。

questions.prompt: Items subject to donation were checked individually against a holding period.
questions.explanation: H按每件接收日期和保留期核捐赠资格，不一次全清。D易腐食物另行处置不走普通期限；其他段无捐赠计时。

questions.prompt: The time of finding an item was kept distinct from the time it reached the office.
questions.explanation: B分别记录发现时刻和送办公室时刻，举早发现晚送例。K是到达月份比较不讲发现与送达差；其他段无这两时点。

questions.prompt: A supervised test could help identify keys without releasing them before a claim was settled.
questions.explanation: G在管控下试验并配另一识别细节，未决前不交出。C一般询问箱内细节，不是钥匙试验；其他段无监督试钥匙。

questions.prompt: A summary allowed for the shorter claiming time available to recently received items.
questions.explanation: K新月底到达者可领取时间短，按到达时期分列，不以总分母掩盖。H保留期用于捐赠非统计返还率；其他段无此统计口径。

questions.prompt: Disposal of a leaking perishable item was recorded instead of treating it like an ordinary stored object.
questions.explanation: D漏午餐容器不与手机衣物久存，记处置及理由。H捐赠织物是耐久品期满；其他段无食物污染处置。

questions.prompt: Different reporting channels led into one system without being treated as evidence of honesty.
questions.explanation: E柜台、电话、在线均入同系统，渠道不代表诚信。I外部运营商记录独立，与同系统渠道不同；其他段无渠道人格推断。

questions.prompt: Some identifying features were left out of announcements so claimants could supply them independently.
questions.explanation: F通告只给大类，隐藏特征留作核验，举划痕位置例。C使用这些信息却未说明公告删去特征的决定；其他段不含公告策略。

units.title: 六级匹配：口述史的两种文本版本
units.instruction: Read the complete article. Match each statement to paragraph A–O. A paragraph may be used more than once or not at all.

materials.title: Listening Between the Lines
materials.text:
This is an original fictional case for reading practice.

A

The harbour-history project at East Fen began by recording retired dock workers talking about ordinary working days. Its organisers expected the recordings to become an archive and a book. Transcription appeared to be a necessary intermediate task, moving spoken words into a form editors could quote and readers could search. During the pilot interviews, however, the team found that a transcript was already an interpretation. Choices about punctuation, pauses and spelling affected how a speaker appeared, even when no whole sentence had been deliberately removed.

B

A pause could indicate hesitation, interruption or a moment spent recalling a name. The project did not mark every brief intake of breath, but it retained pauses that affected how a statement could reasonably be understood. For the reading edition, repetitive starts were sometimes shortened, with that editorial practice explained at the front. The research transcript preserved more of the spoken sequence. Neither edition was presented as the recording itself. A cleaner page could aid reading without becoming the single complete form of the interview.

C

Editors initially corrected unfamiliar grammar into the standard form used in the project office. Several speakers objected that the result no longer sounded like them. The team revised its policy, preserving distinctive constructions while avoiding exaggerated spelling that turned an accent into a visual performance. Nonstandard grammar was not labelled evidence of poor understanding or weak memory. The aim was to retain features of voice without inviting readers to treat distance from the office’s preferred English as a measure of the speaker’s intelligence.

D

Permission was recorded at the level of an interview segment rather than assumed to cover everything said during one session. A speaker might approve public discussion of dock work but restrict a passage about a living neighbour. The catalogue could still state that the interview existed while the relevant audio remained unavailable to ordinary users. Staff explained the difference between discoverable metadata and permission to listen. A public title was not a promise that all the material beneath it had been cleared for unrestricted access.

E

Translating a family term created a different kind of uncertainty. One expression referred to a relationship that the project’s main language did not divide in the same way. Instead of choosing an apparently neat equivalent and hiding the difficulty, the editor retained the source term with an explanation. The note did not establish that every speaker in the region used the word identically. It described the usage in this interview and named the person who had explained it, leaving room for other accounts elsewhere.

F

Quotations in the book included segment identifiers and time references. These had to be tested against the archived audio, because a player that skipped an introductory announcement displayed a different starting point from one that included it. A reader needed a route back to the intended passage, not a number copied from whichever player happened to be open on an editor’s laptop. The project therefore defined its timing reference and checked sample citations after files were prepared for public use, rather than assuming every interface counted from the same point.

G

Full-text search created an access problem. A restricted passage could remain hidden in the audio player yet appear word for word in search-result previews if its transcript had been indexed without the same controls. The team therefore applied permissions to the search index as well as to the media files. A withheld segment could not leak simply because a public user entered a distinctive phrase. Making a file inaccessible was insufficient if another representation of its contents remained openly retrievable through a different part of the service.

H

Automatic transcription worked unevenly across the recordings. Overall accuracy looked acceptable, but one group of speakers with a particular accent had many more errors. Short, noisy passages also performed differently from long studio interviews. Reporting a single average would have hidden who needed more editorial attention. The project reviewed samples separately by recording conditions and speaking patterns, while avoiding the claim that a small pilot established a permanent ranking of accents. The relevant question was how this system performed on these recordings, not which voices were intrinsically clearer.

I

Two workers gave conflicting accounts of the same strike meeting. The editors did not combine their recollections into a sentence that neither had spoken. They presented the accounts with dates and attribution, and noted the disagreement. Where independent documents existed, a separate note described them. Remembering an event was itself valuable historical material, but the sincerity of a recollection did not guarantee every detail. The archive could preserve a disagreement without pretending either that both versions were identical or that a transcript alone could resolve which was correct.

J

Digital preservation included checking stored files against recorded checksums. A match helped show that a file had not changed in the storage process. It did not show that the interviewee’s account was factually accurate, that the microphone had captured every word, or that a transcript had interpreted it correctly. The technical check answered a narrow question about the stored object’s integrity. Staff kept that assurance separate from judgements about evidence, resisting an attractive but misleading claim that a verified file was therefore verified history.

K

Some participants chose to appear under pseudonyms. The link between a public name and contact details was kept separately with restricted staff access. Editors also checked the narrative for indirect clues that could defeat the chosen anonymity, such as a uniquely identifying combination of job, date and address. Replacing a person’s name did not automatically make the account anonymous. The team discussed these limits with participants rather than treating the pseudonym field as a switch that could guarantee privacy regardless of what the rest of the interview revealed.

L

Payment for transcription was initially estimated from audio duration. An hour of clear conversation between two speakers could require less work than an hour full of overlapping voices and unfamiliar names. The team adjusted its budgeting categories to recognise that difference. It did not reward someone for producing more words through unnecessary repetition or assume slow completion showed inexperience. Work estimates included the difficulty of checking uncertain passages. This gave the project a more realistic account of labour than a flat rate that treated all recorded minutes as interchangeable units.

M

A participant later withdrew permission for one public segment under the terms agreed at the start. The public record explained that the passage was no longer available, so an old citation did not silently lead to a different quotation. Staff followed the agreed retention rules for internal copies rather than assuming that withdrawal either required universal erasure or permitted indefinite private retention. The notice preserved a trace of the change without repeating the restricted content. What remained accessible was determined by the consent arrangement, not by the convenience of the website.

N

For an exhibition, curators proposed a dramatic thirty-second audio extract. The speaker approved its words but said that, without the following sentence, it sounded like praise for an employer he had actually criticised. The extract was revised and reviewed again. Approval of an interview for archive access did not automatically settle the meaning of a new montage. Selecting a fragment created a fresh context, so the project checked the relationship between the extract and the larger exchange rather than relying only on the accuracy of the isolated words.

O

The finished project offered a readable selection alongside more detailed research transcripts and recordings, subject to their respective permissions. It explained how the versions differed and who had made the editorial choices. The organisers no longer described the process as simply converting sound into text. They had constructed several ways of encountering the interviews, each with a purpose and a limit. Accountability depended on making those purposes visible and preserving routes between the permitted versions, so that editorial convenience did not quietly become the authority of the archive.

questions.prompt: A speaker’s departure from a preferred language form was not treated as evidence of inferior intelligence.
questions.explanation: C明确非标准语法不表示理解差，并反对以办公室英语距离衡量智力。H讨论识别软件差错，不评价语法与智力；其他段无此判断。

questions.prompt: A successful technical integrity test did not establish the historical truth of an account.
questions.explanation: J校验和只能说明文件存储未变，不能证明口述事实真。F是引文时间定位可靠性，不是文件完整性与史实区分；其他段无checksum论证。

questions.prompt: An aggregate performance score hid unequal error rates for different voices and recording conditions.
questions.explanation: H整体自动转写准确度掩盖口音及噪声分组误差。L工作时长估费差异不是识别准确率；其他段无分组系统错误分析。

questions.prompt: An interview could have a publicly discoverable record while some of its audio remained restricted.
questions.explanation: D区分公开目录元数据与片段听取许可。G搜索索引权限防泄露不是首先规定存在可发现但音频受限；其他段无这套目录访问界线。

questions.prompt: An extract containing accurate words was revised because removing its context changed its apparent stance.
questions.explanation: N三十秒选段字句准确但缺下一句像赞雇主，重选再审。B为可读版删口头重复，不讲立场反转的展览剪辑；其他段无该例。

questions.prompt: Citation times were checked because playback interfaces could use different starting points.
questions.explanation: F播放器是否计片头导致时间起点不同，定义时间基准并抽检。J校验文件无变不检查播放器计时；其他段无起点误差。

questions.prompt: Incompatible memories were attributed separately rather than merged into a statement no participant had made.
questions.explanation: I罢工会议两口述冲突保留归属不合并，可另注文献。E翻译亲属词只是词义差异；其他段无冲突事件记忆拼合。

questions.prompt: Budgeting recognised that equal audio durations could require different amounts of checking work.
questions.explanation: L明确清楚对话与重叠陌生名同一小时工量不同。H分组识别误差可能相关但无费用工时规则；其他段无劳动估价。

questions.prompt: Access restrictions were applied to a search index to prevent hidden content appearing through previews.
questions.explanation: G受限音频若转写已索引会在结果预览泄露，权限须贯穿索引。D目录存在信息可公开不等于内容，未描述索引泄露；其他段无此路径。

questions.prompt: A changed public permission left a notice rather than silently redirecting an old citation to different content.
questions.explanation: M撤许可后公示片段不可用，旧引用不暗指另一引文，按同意条款管理内部留存。D初始授权不处理事后变更；其他段无撤后公告。

units.title: 六级匹配：街道阴影地图的测量边界
units.instruction: Read the complete article. Match each statement to paragraph A–O. A paragraph may be used more than once or not at all.

materials.title: The Shade That Moved
materials.text:
This is an original fictional case for reading practice.

A

The fictional city of Carden wanted to identify walking routes that remained usable during hot afternoons. Its first proposal was to map the number of trees on every street. The count was easy to explain and already existed in a maintenance database. Yet a street with many young trees could offer little shelter at the time walkers needed it. The planning group expanded the project from a tree inventory to an account of where shade fell, when it appeared and whether people could actually occupy the shaded space.

B

The same tree cast different shadows during the day. A mark placed beside its trunk did not describe the position of its shade at three o’clock. Surveyors recorded the time of each observation and the side of the street where the shadow lay. They also noted building orientation. A route described as shaded in the morning could expose walkers later, even though none of the trees had moved. The team therefore published time-specific layers rather than a single permanent line supposedly representing the experience of all pedestrians.

C

Buildings and temporary structures could provide shade as well as vegetation. The survey recorded their contributions separately, because each involved different ownership, maintenance and seasonal questions. A covered walkway did not become a tree benefit merely because a tree stood nearby. Conversely, an absence of trees did not prove that a street offered no shelter. Keeping the sources distinct let planners discuss several ways of improving a route without forcing every existing patch of shade into the same policy category or treating all shade providers as interchangeable objects.

D

Volunteers also collected thermal images of surfaces. Two pictures with dramatic red and blue areas appeared easy to compare, but their display scales had been set differently. The same colour could correspond to different temperature ranges. Before including a side-by-side comparison, the team checked the measurement settings and used a shared scale where comparison was appropriate. A vivid colour contrast was not itself evidence of a larger temperature difference. The image needed its numerical context, particularly when viewers had no reason to know how the display had been configured.

E

The first walking surveys followed streets already used by the volunteers. These were convenient and familiar, but did not form a representative sample of the whole city. Industrial edges, steep streets and areas distant from the volunteers’ homes received little attention. The project recruited additional participants and published the observation coverage. It did not repair the gap by assuming unvisited places resembled the nearest surveyed street. A map could be useful while incomplete, provided it showed which parts of the city had actually contributed evidence.

F

One shaded route looked excellent on a map until a wheelchair user tried to follow it. At a narrow point, bins occupied the shaded pavement, leaving passage available only on the sunnier side. The survey then distinguished shade falling on the street from accessible shade along a continuous path. Observers recorded obstacles and crossings, rather than merely adding the total shadow area on both sides. A patch of shelter could exist physically yet fail to provide a practical option for someone moving through the route in a particular way.

G

Several privately operated cafés had sheltered seating. The team recorded whether sitting there required a purchase and when the premises opened. It did not add every shaded chair to a total of freely available public resting places. Nor did it exclude all private locations from the descriptive map: they could still be useful to some walkers under stated conditions. The important distinction was between the presence of shade and the terms on which a person could use it. A shaded seat behind a closed door was not available simply because it appeared in a photograph.

H

Season affected the observations. Leaf cover and the sun’s position changed, and one survey week could not represent every month. The city arranged repeat visits and attached dates to the layers. Where winter observations were missing, the team resisted copying a summer result into that season. This did not require waiting years before publishing anything. It required describing the period to which a finding applied and updating the record when further observations arrived. A date was part of the evidence, rather than a decorative caption on an otherwise timeless map.

I

Walkers were invited to describe comfort, not only temperature. Some valued a sheltered place to pause, while others wanted an uninterrupted route. The project retained these different experiences rather than translating every account into one numerical score. It did not infer that a preference voiced by several participants belonged automatically to everyone of the same age or background. Individual reports could reveal needs worth investigating without becoming a ready-made rule about an entire population. The planners used them to ask more specific questions at later meetings.

J

Collecting walking routes risked revealing more than environmental conditions. A line beginning repeatedly at one doorway could identify someone’s home. Public displays therefore used combined route information and omitted fine detail that was unnecessary for the shade analysis. Researchers kept access to the original traces limited. They also explained that removing names alone would not make every movement record anonymous. The privacy decision concerned what a path could reveal through its pattern, not merely whether the file contained an obvious field labelled with the participant’s identity.

K

The budget discussion included responsibility for upkeep. A proposed shade structure required someone to inspect fittings, clear debris and deal with damage. Its purchase price did not cover all those obligations. The team named the organisation expected to maintain each option and included continuing costs in the estimate. An apparently inexpensive installation could become unusable if nobody accepted those duties. This did not prove that permanent structures were always worse than planting. It made the comparison more complete by showing which responsibilities accompanied different proposals after the opening day.

L

Temporary parasols were tested at a small square before a permanent arrangement was chosen. Their positions could be changed in response to observations. The trial helped identify useful locations for a few seats, but it could not establish how the whole surrounding district would feel after a much larger redesign. Staff reported what the small intervention had tested and where extrapolation would begin. The ability to move a parasol was valuable precisely because it allowed correction; it was not evidence that the first layout had been correct in every possible setting.

M

To investigate the effect of a newly planted row of trees, analysts compared observations with another street. They checked whether traffic, building work and surface materials had changed at the same time. A cooler reading after planting was relevant, but it could not automatically be attributed entirely to the new trees. The comparison street also had to be described rather than treated as a perfect copy of the project site. The study reported remaining differences, allowing readers to assess how much confidence to place in the proposed explanation.

N

Blank areas on the map caused repeated misunderstanding. Some readers assumed that an uncoloured street had no shade. In fact, several blanks indicated that nobody had surveyed the place at the relevant hour. The team introduced separate symbols for observed absence and missing observation. It kept this distinction in downloadable data as well as in the display, so later analysts would not silently convert unknown values to zero. A visually simple map was less useful than a slightly more complex one that did not confuse lack of evidence with evidence of lack.

O

The final public meeting concerned priorities as much as measurement. A plan focused on the route to a clinic could differ from one aimed at increasing the total shaded area across the city. Neither goal could be selected by measuring shadow accurately enough. The report stated which objective a recommendation served and who had participated in choosing it. Technical information could help compare consequences under a goal, but it could not make that goal disappear. The map became accountable when the choices behind its recommendations remained open to public examination.

questions.prompt: The map distinguished an unmeasured location from a location where shade had been observed to be absent.
questions.explanation: N空白有未测与实测无阴两种，图和下载数据均分码。E抽样覆盖不全是原因背景，但未说明缺测与零值不同符号；其他段无该编码区分。

questions.prompt: Different display settings could make the same colour misleading in a comparison of images.
questions.explanation: D热图标尺不同，同色可指不同温度，比较须核数值设置。B时段图层是日影移动而非色标；其他段无热图色标问题。

questions.prompt: A shaded place was described together with conditions such as payment and opening hours.
questions.explanation: G咖啡座须否购买及营业时间，区分有阴与可用条件。F谈障碍通行不是消费条件；其他段无付费营业组合。

questions.prompt: A tree’s fixed location did not establish where its shadow would be at a later hour.
questions.explanation: B树没动但早午阴影不同，需时刻和街侧记录。H季节差异不是同日时刻移动；其他段无树位与影位的具体关系。

questions.prompt: Changes occurring alongside planting were examined before crediting the planting with a cooler reading.
questions.explanation: M比较新树与对照街，核同期交通施工路面变化，避免全归因树。K比较养护成本不是降温因果；其他段无同期混杂因素。

questions.prompt: A physical obstruction prevented an apparently shaded route from functioning as an accessible path.
questions.explanation: F轮椅遇垃圾桶占阴侧，需到晒侧，故记录连续可通行阴影。G门关座位是使用许可条件非路面障碍行进；其他段无轮椅路径实测。

questions.prompt: Comparing proposals required identifying who would accept maintenance duties after installation.
questions.explanation: K列采购外检查清理损坏责任及持续费用，指定养护组织。C仅区分遮阴来源，不规定新设施后续责任；其他段无这组预算义务。

questions.prompt: Findings were dated and revisited rather than automatically extended from one season to another.
questions.explanation: H叶量日位随季节变，复访并保留日期，不套夏季到冬季。B是日内时间，E地域样本，均非跨季延伸；其他段无该处理。

questions.prompt: Public route data were reduced because travel patterns could identify people even without names.
questions.explanation: J路径起点可暴露住址，公开合并淡化、原始限权，不以去名保匿名。I人群偏好不可泛化是推断边界非移动隐私；其他段无轨迹去识别问题。

questions.prompt: Selecting the goal of a recommendation remained a public judgement that accurate measurement alone could not settle.
questions.explanation: O去诊所路线与全市总阴影是不同目标，准确测量不能自动选目标，须公示参与和目的。A扩展树数为阴影量只是测量口径起点；其他段无最终公共目标选择。

units.title: 四级选词：一本手工书的页序
units.instruction: Read the complete passage. Choose an unchanged word from the shared bank for each gap. Each of the fifteen words may be used at most once; five words are not needed.

materials.title: Before the Book Has a Cover
materials.text:
At a student bookmaking class, a large sheet of paper was ____1____ down the middle, bringing one half over the other. Several sheets prepared this way formed small groups called ____2____. These groups would later be sewn together to make a book. A stack of loose single pages required a different method, so the tutor kept the two examples apart.

Before any sewing, the pages were ____3____ in pencil from first to last. This helped students detect an upside-down group or a missing leaf. The groups were then ____4____ along the folded edge, with their edges brought into the same line rather than left unevenly placed.

The fold was carefully ____5____ at marked points to make the small holes needed for thread. The tutor demonstrated the tools and supervised their use. A student could practise on spare paper before working on the pages intended for the final book.

During sewing, the ____6____ of the thread mattered: too much pulling force could tear a hole, while too little left the groups loose. The completed ____7____ held the pages together. It was not simply decoration along the outside of a stack.

Only after checking that every group was in the correct order did the class cut the uneven outer edges. They were ____8____ to give the book a neat outline. The text had been printed with generous ____9____, blank spaces around the writing, so this cutting would not remove words.

Finally, a protective ____10____ was attached around the pages. Its size was checked against the finished book rather than guessed from the first loose sheet. Students opened their books carefully and examined whether the pages turned freely. A handsome outside could not compensate for a missing page or a structure that pulled apart when read.

questions.prompt: Before the Book Has a Cover: choose the unchanged word for gap 1.
questions.explanation: bringing one half over other直接定义folded折叠。trimmed是裁边、pierced为穿孔，aligned为对齐，均不表示对折动作；woven是编织而非纸半边翻覆。

questions.prompt: Before the Book Has a Cover: choose the unchanged word for gap 2.
questions.explanation: 文中明确给成组折页命名signatures书帖。binding为装订整体，margins是空白边，cover是封面，grain为纸纹；其余不指这些待缝的复数组。

questions.prompt: Before the Book Has a Cover: choose the unchanged word for gap 3.
questions.explanation: in pencil from first to last及detect missing leaf要求依次编号numbered。folded/trimmed/pierced不产生首尾序号，aligned只排齐；其他词不作该被动编号动作。

questions.prompt: Before the Book Has a Cover: choose the unchanged word for gap 4.
questions.explanation: edges brought into same line定义aligned对齐。trimmed为切齐但此步只放齐，后文才裁边；folded为折叠，pierced穿孔，woven编织，均非所述位置调整。

questions.prompt: Before the Book Has a Cover: choose the unchanged word for gap 5.
questions.explanation: make small holes needed for thread定义pierced穿孔。trimmed是裁去边缘、folded是折，aligned对齐，woven编织不适用于造针孔；其他候选不表该动作。

questions.prompt: Before the Book Has a Cover: choose the unchanged word for gap 6.
questions.explanation: too much pulling force与too little定义线张力tension。binding是装订结构，grain纸纹，adhesive胶、margins留白，均非线的拉力；其他项词性或含义不合。

questions.prompt: Before the Book Has a Cover: choose the unchanged word for gap 7.
questions.explanation: held pages together的完成装订为binding。cover此时未附，后段才做保护外层；signatures是被装订的组，adhesive在本案例缝线工序非主体，tension是力而非结构。

questions.prompt: Before the Book Has a Cover: choose the unchanged word for gap 8.
questions.explanation: cut uneven outer edges、neat outline要求trimmed修裁。pierced只打孔，folded折页，aligned摆齐，woven编织均不切掉边缘；其他词不作该切边被动。

questions.prompt: Before the Book Has a Cover: choose the unchanged word for gap 9.
questions.explanation: blank spaces around writing直接定义margins页边留白。cover外壳、binding装订、grain纸纹不表文字周围空白；signatures为折页组，其他词非此复数名词。

questions.prompt: Before the Book Has a Cover: choose the unchanged word for gap 10.
questions.explanation: protective且attached around pages、outside指cover封面。binding是页组连接非后附外罩，signatures为内页，adhesive是胶不作为整块尺寸核对保护层；其他候选不指外封。

units.title: 四级选词：拉链为何能合上
units.instruction: Read the complete passage. Choose an unchanged word from the shared bank for each gap. Each of the fifteen words may be used at most once; five words are not needed.

materials.title: The Small Piece That Joins Two Rows
materials.text:
A zip fastener joins two edges by bringing rows of small ____1____ together. These projecting pieces are not all shaped identically across different products, but each row must fit the other. The small moving part held by the pull tab is called the ____2____. As it travels, it guides the two rows into the required position.

In a working zip, the pieces ____3____ with one another, fitting together so that the rows hold. Moving the guide in the opposite direction leaves the rows ____4____ again, no longer joined along that section. This joining process is normally ____5____: it can be undone and repeated without destroying the fastener.

A beginner sometimes pulls harder when the guide stops. That can place unnecessary ____6____ on the fastener, exposing it to a force that may damage the pieces or their attachment. The cause might instead be fabric ____7____ inside the moving part, trapped where it should not be.

In a clothing-care class, the tutor demonstrated how to stop and examine a snag rather than keep pulling. She eased the fabric out ____8____, carefully and with little force. The aim was not to turn a small obstruction into a torn lining.

Before closing an open-ended jacket zip, its starting sections had to be ____9____, positioned correctly in relation to each other. Pulling from a poor starting position could not make that initial fit correct. For a suitable product, its care instructions might also recommend a substance to ____10____ the moving parts, reducing friction by making their contact more slippery.

The tutor stressed that damage could take different forms. A missing piece, trapped cloth and an incorrectly started jacket were not one identical problem. Knowing the names of the parts helped learners describe what they could see before deciding whether an adjustment, a repair or replacement was appropriate.

questions.prompt: The Small Piece That Joins Two Rows: choose the unchanged word for gap 1.
questions.explanation: small projecting pieces in two rows为teeth拉链齿。slider是单一滑块非复数突出件；strain是受力、patent专利不指此部件，其他候选非该复数名词。

questions.prompt: The Small Piece That Joins Two Rows: choose the unchanged word for gap 2.
questions.explanation: held by pull tab、guides rows的移动件定义slider滑块。teeth为两排齿，不是拉片握持的单一导件；patent是权利、strain为力，其他项不命名该部件。

questions.prompt: The Small Piece That Joins Two Rows: choose the unchanged word for gap 3.
questions.explanation: fitting together so rows hold定义interlock咬合。yield为让步或屈服，与两排相互扣住不同；lubricate为润滑，不能与one another在此表示齿咬合；其他候选非该复数主语原形动作。

questions.prompt: The Small Piece That Joins Two Rows: choose the unchanged word for gap 4.
questions.explanation: no longer joined直接说明separated分离。aligned只说排齐，不等于解开；caught为卡住，woven为织在一起，均不表示反方向打开的结果；reversible只是可逆特性。

questions.prompt: The Small Piece That Joins Two Rows: choose the unchanged word for gap 5.
questions.explanation: undone and repeated without destroying定义reversible可逆。fragile为易损不等于可反复撤销；woven表编织，aligned位置对齐，其他词不命名这一过程性质。

questions.prompt: The Small Piece That Joins Two Rows: choose the unchanged word for gap 6.
questions.explanation: unnecessary strain及force may damage定义过大应力。patent为专利，slider为实体部件，teeth为齿，不是施加于拉链的力；其他项非该受力名词。

questions.prompt: The Small Piece That Joins Two Rows: choose the unchanged word for gap 7.
questions.explanation: trapped where should not be定义caught夹住。woven指本来织成，aligned说对齐、separated分开都不是织物误卡在滑块；fragile虽可形容织物却不解释trapped。

questions.prompt: The Small Piece That Joins Two Rows: choose the unchanged word for gap 8.
questions.explanation: carefully and little force直接释义gently轻柔。consistently表一致地，不能表低力度，且与阻碍处理关系不如后置定义；其余候选不作该动作方式副词。

questions.prompt: The Small Piece That Joins Two Rows: choose the unchanged word for gap 9.
questions.explanation: positioned correctly in relation定义aligned对齐。separated只分离、caught卡住、woven织造都不等于正确起始匹配；reversible说过程可逆而非两起始端位置。

questions.prompt: The Small Piece That Joins Two Rows: choose the unchanged word for gap 10.
questions.explanation: reducing friction by more slippery定义lubricate润滑。interlock咬合不等于减摩、yield屈服，均不指涂合宜物质减小接触摩擦；其他词非recommend substance to后的该原形动作。

units.title: 六级选词：乐谱作者署名的证据
units.instruction: Read the complete passage. Choose an unchanged word from the shared bank for each gap. Each of the fifteen words may be used at most once; five words are not needed.

materials.title: Whose Notes Are These?
materials.text:
A fictional music archive received an unsigned manuscript thought to be connected with a known composer. Its catalogue editor treated the proposed ____1____, the assignment of authorship, as a question requiring evidence rather than an attractive label. The presence of familiar musical phrases did not settle who had written the piece.

The manuscript was not established as an ____2____, a score in the composer’s own hand. It might instead have been produced by a copyist. Other handwritten ____3____, duplicate transcriptions of the same music, survived in different collections, and their differences showed that the work had circulated in more than one written form.

Crossed-out passages and replacement notes revealed ____4____ within the newly received manuscript. These changes were valuable evidence about a process, but the editor could not assume that the person making them was necessarily the original composer. A performer might also alter a passage for a particular occasion.

The team examined the ____5____ of the documents, their order in time. A dated performance notice helped establish that one version existed before a later copy was made. This did not by itself show which surviving sheet was the first physical record.

They also investigated ____6____, the history of ownership and custody through which the manuscript had reached the archive. An undocumented gap in that history was marked rather than filled with an invented link. Analysis of the musical language was described as ____7____, concerned with style rather than the identity of the handwriting.

A matching independent reference could offer ____8____ for a proposed connection, supporting it with evidence from another source. In its absence, part of the account remained ____9____, based on an informed supposition rather than an established fact. The catalogue stated that limit explicitly.

The final entry explained how the music might have been ____10____ from one person or collection to another. It offered a reasoned account of circulation while leaving the authorship question open. A useful catalogue did not need to transform every uncertain relationship into a confident name.

questions.prompt: Whose Notes Are These?: choose the unchanged word for gap 1.
questions.explanation: assignment of authorship明确定义attribution署名归属。annotation为注释、chronology年代顺序、provenance保管来源、corroboration佐证都不直接等于把作品归给某作者。

questions.prompt: Whose Notes Are These?: choose the unchanged word for gap 2.
questions.explanation: score in composer’s own hand定义autograph作曲者亲笔谱。copies为复数抄本，annotation注记、attribution归属都不是以an开头的亲笔文献名；其他候选不符合此释义。

questions.prompt: Whose Notes Are These?: choose the unchanged word for gap 3.
questions.explanation: Other handwritten加复数及duplicate transcriptions直接定义copies抄本。revisions是改动，不等同此处定义的重复誊写文本；第4空另由划去替换明确占用revisions。其他候选抽象单数或词性不合，不能指这些完整抄谱。

questions.prompt: Whose Notes Are These?: choose the unchanged word for gap 4.
questions.explanation: crossed-out passages and replacement notes为revisions修改。copies指多份文献不是一稿内部划改，annotation虽可指注释但此处复数形式不匹配且非删除替换；其他名词不命名改稿动作。

questions.prompt: Whose Notes Are These?: choose the unchanged word for gap 5.
questions.explanation: their order in time定义chronology时序。provenance是所有和保管历史，attribution作者判断、corroboration佐证、annotation注释均非文献先后序。

questions.prompt: Whose Notes Are These?: choose the unchanged word for gap 6.
questions.explanation: history ownership and custody定义provenance来源流转。chronology纯先后、attribution作者归属都不完整表达谁持有如何入馆；annotation/corroboration不指保管沿革。

questions.prompt: Whose Notes Are These?: choose the unchanged word for gap 7.
questions.explanation: concerned with style rather than handwriting定义stylistic风格分析。distinctive只是独特、recurrent反复、conjectural推测、unequivocal明确，都不说明研究对象为风格；副词不作此描述补语。

questions.prompt: Whose Notes Are These?: choose the unchanged word for gap 8.
questions.explanation: supporting with evidence another source说明corroboration佐证。attribution是待支持判断，provenance流转史，annotation注记、chronology年代序都不直接指独立印证。

questions.prompt: Whose Notes Are These?: choose the unchanged word for gap 9.
questions.explanation: informed supposition rather than established fact直接定义conjectural推测性的。unequivocal与未确事实冲突，distinctive独特、recurrent反复、stylistic风格均不表达证据尚属推测。

questions.prompt: Whose Notes Are These?: choose the unchanged word for gap 10.
questions.explanation: from person or collection to another及circulation指transmitted传递流转。revisions为名词、copies也是名词；其他候选不作have been后的这一被动传递分词，independently副词不能单作谓语。

units.title: 六级选词：跨币种项目预算的比较日期
units.instruction: Read the complete passage. Choose an unchanged word from the shared bank for each gap. Each of the fifteen words may be used at most once; five words are not needed.

materials.title: The Rate on the Budget Sheet
materials.text:
A fictional research consortium bought equipment priced in one currency while receiving its grant in another. Its first budget table listed amounts without naming their currency ____1____, the monetary unit in which each figure was expressed. A total that silently added unlike units looked precise but had no clear interpretation.

The finance officer therefore ____2____ every quoted price into the grant currency using a stated rate. She recorded the date and the source of that rate. Payment would occur later, so this budget conversion did not establish the amount that would actually leave the account at ____3____, the completion of payment to the supplier.

A ____4____ of future costs was presented as an estimate rather than an amount already paid. One source of variation was exchange-rate ____5____, the tendency for the rate to fluctuate over time. Replacing the printed estimate with more decimal places would not remove that movement.

For part of the purchase, the consortium ____6____ its currency exposure through a contract fixing a rate. This arrangement reduced a specified risk within its agreed terms; it did not make every project cost certain or remove the need to read the contract. Other purchases remained exposed to changing rates.

The report distinguished an expected saving from a saving actually ____7____ when an exchange was completed. A favourable movement visible on a screen did not automatically become a completed gain for every transaction. The record of ____8____, money spent by the project, was kept separate from quotations for items not yet bought.

The officer also warned that the table showed ____9____ amounts in current money, without adjusting them to represent constant purchasing power across years. That was suitable for some administrative purposes, but not every long-term comparison.

After payment, the team reviewed the original estimate ____10____, looking back with knowledge of the outcome. It kept the dated forecast beside the actual figures. Rewriting the earlier budget as if the final rate had been known from the start would have hidden what uncertainty the decision-makers had genuinely faced.

questions.prompt: The Rate on the Budget Sheet: choose the unchanged word for gap 1.
questions.explanation: monetary unit in which figure expressed定义denomination币种单位。appreciation为升值、liabilities为负债、expenditure支出、accrual应计，均不指表中每数值用的货币单位。

questions.prompt: The Rate on the Budget Sheet: choose the unchanged word for gap 2.
questions.explanation: every price into grant currency说明converted换算。hedged为对冲风险，未必将每项报价按一率换算；yielded为产生不搭此货币转换，realised为实现收益而非所有价格换币，其他非此过去式。

questions.prompt: The Rate on the Budget Sheet: choose the unchanged word for gap 3.
questions.explanation: completion payment to supplier直接定义settlement结算。forecast是预测、accrual应计不是付款完成、volatility波动、appreciation升值，均不等同供应商款项交付完成。

questions.prompt: The Rate on the Budget Sheet: choose the unchanged word for gap 4.
questions.explanation: future costs、estimate rather than already paid定义forecast预测。expenditure为已花支出与未付相反，liabilities负债不等于预计总成本，denomination单位不是未来估算。

questions.prompt: The Rate on the Budget Sheet: choose the unchanged word for gap 5.
questions.explanation: tendency rate fluctuate定义volatility波动性。appreciation只升值单向不是上下变动性质，settlement为结算、accrual为应计、forecast为预测均非波动性。

questions.prompt: The Rate on the Budget Sheet: choose the unchanged word for gap 6.
questions.explanation: currency exposure through rate-fixing contract说明hedged对冲。converted是按当前率换算不保证锁未来，realised是收益已实现不指风险合约，yielded产生不表达保护敞口；其他词非过去式操作。

questions.prompt: The Rate on the Budget Sheet: choose the unchanged word for gap 7.
questions.explanation: actually when exchange completed与expected对照，realised已实现。converted指换算且以saving为宾语会换其表示货币而非确认兑现，hedged为对冲不是兑现节省，其他词不作该实际实现的过去分词。

questions.prompt: The Rate on the Budget Sheet: choose the unchanged word for gap 8.
